title: 2026-06-15-harlequin-health-latency-econ-discovery
summary: Initial latency and throughput discovery for Harlequin Health's real-time clinical summarization feature. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for p95 latency <= 300ms on streaming responses, concurrency targets ~200 simultaneous users, and token/sec throughput for 2k concurrent chats. Discussed VPC/KMS requirements, SOC2, and benchmarking approach; agreed to run a streaming token/sec microbenchmark and share security pack.
topics: p95 latency targets for streaming generation
hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
security: SOC 2, KMS, SSO, audit logs
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-15 09:00 PDT | Duration: 44m | Recording: On
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Sarah (CTO), Rajesh (Lead ML), Jenna (Infra), Omar (PM)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you carving time. quick round intro?
[00:08] Sarah: Hi I'm Sarah CTO at Harlequin, we run a clinical notes product for hospitals.
[00:12] Rajesh: Rajesh, lead on ML infra and production models.
[00:15] Jenna: Jenna on infra, mostly networking and security.
[00:18] Omar: Omar product, driving timelines.
[00:20] Maya: Great. Liam and Carlos from our side, SEs who will nerd out on perf stuff.
[00:26] Liam: hey all, will dive into latency and throughput.

[00:34] Maya: To set context, Harlequin wants real-time summarization of patient-provider chats, streaming token output to the front end. Target p95 latency is pretty tight right? Sarah you mentioned ~200-300ms p95 per token?
[00:46] Sarah: yeah, on live streams we need p95 for user-visible tokens under 300ms ideally. for shorter prompts maybe lower. otherwise clinicians notice lag and UX drops.
[00:57] Rajesh: our peak concurrency estimate is about 150 to 250 active streams during morning rounds, but bursts hit about 2k concurrent short-lived sessions across the org — those are lighter. We're mostly worried about sustained concurrency of ~200.
[01:12] Jenna: and we have strict networking: private VPC peering, no public egress for PHI at rest. KMS must be customer-managed.

[01:22] Liam: okay good. quick framing — we support three deployment modes: Hosted API for quickest time-to-value, Dedicated reserved capacity for predictable throughput, and Private (VPC/on-prem) for strict compliance. Each has tradeoffs for p95, cold starts, and token/sec economics.
[01:40] Carlos: for streaming, the p95 you see in-hosted will depend on model choice and prefix lengths; smaller context and quantized models help. dedicated tilts predictability — consistent p95 under load. private gives full network control but you manage GPUs.

[01:58] Sarah: can you give us numbers? like realistic p95 and tokens/sec per GPU for the popular open models?
[02:05] Liam: sure. rough numbers — for a 13B-ish model on NVidia A100 with our runtime, sustained streaming token generation (greedy) p95 per token under low-latency config can be around 80-120ms; for 70B models it's more like 180-350ms depending on optimization and quantization. those are ballpark and vary by prompt length and kv cache reuse.
[02:28] Rajesh: when you say kv cache reuse, does that mean sessions with similar prefixes get faster?
[02:32] Liam: yes, our prefix/KV caching improves steady state. for conversational flows where the prompt is shared you often see token/sec improve by 20-40% after warmup.

[02:45] Jenna: about concurrency — if we need 200 concurrent steady streams, how many GPUs for dedicated?
02:50] Carlos: depends on model/sequence length. Example: 13B with batch multiplexing and small window might serve ~30-40 concurrent streaming users per A100 with our config. So 200 concurrent would map to ~6-7 GPUs with headroom. For 70B you'd need ~3-4x that.

[03:09] Sarah: and burst to 2k short sessions — do you recommend autoscaling or a hybrid?
[03:14] Liam: hybrid works: Dedicated for steady sustained capacity, hosted burst to handle spikes, or reserved capacity with burst credits. Automatic fallback policy can route to cheaper model variants or hosted pool.

[03:28] Omar: latency across region? our primary is us-west and some east coast hospitals. We need < 50ms network RTT ideally.
[03:35] Liam: network RTT is key. hosting region in the same cloud region reduces network tail. For Private, you'd be on-prem or VPC — network controlled.

[03:45] Sarah: security — SOC2, encryption, audit logs — do you provide SOC 2 docs and customer-managed KMS?
[03:51] Maya: yes, we have SOC 2 Type 2. Customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated options; Hosted also supports envelope encryption with customer keys on request (needs paperwork). Audit logs and token-level tracing available in Redwood Console. we'll send our security pack after the call.

[04:10] Rajesh: okay good. can we talk about benchmark methodology? we'd like to run token/sec streaming microbenchmarks that mimic our muxing and input lengths. what's the recommended harness?
[04:19] Liam: recommended approach: 1) start with a microbenchmark using short prompt lengths representative of clinician queries (avg 40 tokens in prompt, outputs 100 tokens), 2) measure cold start and steady state, 3) run multiplexing tests with your concurrency distribution, 4) measure p95 and tail. We'll provide a reference client open-sourced and an nginx-like load generator.

[04:40] Jenna: what about measuring p95 at token level vs response level? we care about token latency for streaming — the initial token matters for perceived latency.
[04:49] Carlos: agree. measure both: initial token latency and per-token steady state p95. streaming can show lower per-token once kv warmed. We'll instrument with per-token timestamps.

[05:03] Sarah: our tolerance for errors: occasional 400ms spikes okay but not above 600ms frequently. how do you handle graceful degradation?
[05:11] Liam: multiple levers — model fallback to smaller variant, turn on more aggressive quantization, or route to hosted fallback with higher latency but guaranteed availability. Also we can shape traffic at the edge to prioritize critical clinician sessions.

[05:28] Omar: cost question — which is more economical for our profile? heavy steady 200 concurrent plus bursts.
[05:35] Maya: Dedicated with reserved GPUs usually gives best unit economics for heavy steady usage. Hosted is more expensive per token for sustained volumes but lower ops. Private has higher upfront but good long-term if you want control. We'll run a cost model.

[05:48] Rajesh: can you quantify tokens/sec per A100 for our 13B baseline in your runtime?
[05:54] Liam: ballpark: for 13B we often see ~2500-4000 tokens/sec per GPU sustained in non-streaming generation when maximizing throughput. For streaming per-token latencies, the tokens/sec metric is less straightforward — because of tail and multiplexing overheads. But you can think of effective user streams: ~30-40 concurrent streams per GPU if outputs are ~100 tokens at interactive latency targets.

[06:18] Sarah: hmm ok. We need to validate with our prompt mixes. Can Redwood run a benchmark on our behalf in hosted and dedicated to show comparatives?
[06:26] Maya: yes we can run a joint benchmark. For hosted we'll run against the hosted pool with your prompts (sanitized). For Dedicated we'll provision a reserved pool and run identical load. For Private we'd provide a reference runner you can run in your env or a partner can run on-prem.

[06:42] Jenna: network constraints — we need traffic to stay inside our VPC, no internet egress. For Dedicated can you do VPC peering?
[06:49] Carlos: Dedicated and Private both support VPC peering. For Hosted we can do private link-ish setups in some clouds via marketplace, but hosted by default goes through Redwood endpoints — would need an architecture review.

[07:02] Rajesh: any caveats with streaming and TLS handshake overhead? we aim for long-lived websockets.
[07:08] Liam: websockets/socket streaming is the best for token-level latency. TLS handshake overhead is only at session start; long-lived sessions amortize that cost. Our runtime supports persistent connections and multiplexing for efficiency.

[07:20] Sarah: do you have any customer references in healthcare who run streaming clinical flows?
[07:24] Maya: yes, a couple—can't share PII on call but we'll include redacted references in the security pack.

[07:33] Omar: timeline — we want to pilot Q3, production by Q4. Anything that would block?
[07:38] Maya: typical next steps are security review, run benchmarks, and pilot contract for Dedicated or Hosted pilot. Should fit Q3 if security review finishes in 2–3 weeks.

[07:50] Rajesh: technical nit — how do you handle KV cache persistence across failover? if a worker dies mid-session do we lose context and does that spike latency?
[07:59] Liam: KV cache is in-memory on the worker for fastest access. We support sticky routing to keep sessions on the same worker; for failover we rehydrate from the request context which adds overhead. In Dedicated we can configure cross-worker checkpointing at some cost; we'll show your options in the benchmark.

[08:19] Jenna: audit logs — do you provide immutable append-only logs that we can ingest into our SIEM?
[08:25] Carlos: yes, audit logs with different retention tiers; we can push to your cloud bucket or stream to SIEM. That's configurable per account.

[08:36] Sarah: let's talk SLOs. We likely need an SLA for p95 targets and uptime. What's Redwood's standard SLA for Dedicated?
[08:44] Maya: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency SLOs in enterprise contracts; exact wording is negotiated. Hosted has standard availability guarantees. We'll introduce legal and SRE in the next meeting to iron SLA specifics.

[08:58] Omar: okay can we get a simple test plan and a price estimate for a 3-month pilot (Dedicated with 8 GPUs + hosted burst)?
[09:06] Maya: yes we'll produce a pilot proposal with cost and test plan.

[09:10] Carlos: on benchmarking specifics — we'll need a representative prompt set, concurrency distribution, and a script for token-level timestamps. If you can share a sanitized sample dataset we can run realistic tests.

[09:24] Rajesh: shareable, yes. We will sanitize. we have a set of 500 prompts typical of morning rounds.

[09:30] Liam: perfect, that will give us a good distribution. We'll run cold-start, steady-state, and burst tests. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 at token-level and response-level, plus token/sec.

[09:43] Sarah: question on function calling and structured outputs — we rely on deterministic JSON chunks. Does streaming split JSON objects mid-token and how to guarantee parsing?
[09:52] Liam: we support structured streaming with chunk boundaries and heuristics to avoid breaking tokens in the middle of JSON. Also function calling can be done server-side and we can return structured deltas. We'll demo that if needed.

[10:05] Omar: any pitfalls you've seen with hospital networks (TLS proxies, deep packet inspection) that affect websockets?
[10:12] Carlos: enterprise middleboxes sometimes terminate websockets or inject delays. Long-lived TLS is best and for worst-case we support fallback to short-polling, albeit with increased latency. Work with your infra to allow persistent websockets to Redwood endpoints over TLS.

[10:28] Rajesh: ok. can you summarize the concrete deliverables after this call?
[10:33] Maya: yes — we'll send: (1) security pack (SOC2, encryption, KMS details, audit logs), (2) pilot proposal w/ cost for 3 months Dedicated 8 GPUs + hosted burst, (3) benchmark plan and runner repo, (4) contract/SLAs template to review.

[10:49] Sarah: timeline for these?
[10:51] Maya: security pack and pilot proposal within 3 business days; benchmark runner and instructions within 5; set up architecture review meeting next week.

[10:58] Jenna: one more: SSO — we use SAML and SCIM for provisioning.
[11:03] Carlos: supported. We'll include SAML/SCIM docs.

[11:10] Omar: ok that's the gist. any final questions?
[11:14] Rajesh: one micro thing — tokenization differences matter for token/sec. which tokenizer are you using in the hosted models?
[11:19] Liam: we track model tokenizer, which can be GPT-like BPE or custom. We'll align on tokenizer in the benchmark to avoid mismatches.

[11:29] Sarah: great thanks.
[11:31] Maya: thanks all. we'll follow up with the pack.

[11:36] [Meeting end]
